vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to be the small thing that makes a bigger thing start
to finally start working, after a period of confusion
a series of things that happen in a fixed order
exactly when something happens, used to join two events

paras: Marina was seventeen when she stopped playing volleyball, and she remembers the exact moment. The moment the coach read out the list for the state team, she knew her name was not on it. She had trained six days a week since she was twelve, so the news did not feel like a disappointment. It felt like a door closing on a room she had lived in for five years.

Her first year of cursinho did not go well. Although she studied more hours than anyone in her class, her results hardly moved, and it took her months to understand why. Whereas volleyball had given every day a clear sequence — warm-up, drills, game — studying had no shape at all. She sat down at eight in the morning and stood up at eleven at night, and nothing in between preceded or followed anything else.

So she built the sequence herself. She divided the day into blocks of ninety minutes so that every subject had a start and an end, and she never let two difficult subjects overlap. She also stopped trying to study and answer messages simultaneously. As soon as one block finished, she walked once around the building before the next one started. It sounds small. Her teachers say it triggered the biggest change in her results that year.

By the time the exam arrived, she had stopped counting hours. She says the real change did not coincide with any test or any grade. It came on an ordinary Tuesday, when she noticed she was tired in the way she used to be tired after a game. “As long as I was tired like that,” she says, “I knew the day had been real.” She passed the following January. Everything fell into place, she says, once she stopped studying like a student and started training like an athlete.
reading.source: A composite portrait of a former athlete preparing for the vestibular, written for this lesson.

To show how giving her day a fixed sequence, like training, changed her results.
To explain how the state volleyball team is selected.

items.situation: Finish this about your own future: By the time the vestibular is over...
tips: By the time the vestibular is over, I will have studied for two years.
After by the time, the present simple. The future goes in the other half.

items.situation: Say what you will do as soon as you get your results.
tips: As soon as I get my results, I will call my parents.
As soon as + present simple, never as soon as I will get.

items.situation: Give a reason with since, in a slightly formal way.
tips: Since I have already chosen medicine, I do not apply for anything else.
Since here means because, not since a date.

items.situation: Say why you study in blocks, with a purpose clause.
tips: I study in blocks so that every subject has an end.
So that + a full clause. In order to + a verb.

items.situation: Contrast basketball and studying in one sentence, with whereas.
tips: Whereas basketball had a clear routine, studying had none at first.
Whereas compares two facts side by side.

items.situation: Correct this out loud: When I will finish the cursinho, I will travel.
tips: When I finish the cursinho, I will travel.
No will inside a time clause about the future.

listenings.text: When I retired from swimming at twenty, the hardest thing was not the training I had lost. It was the shape of the day. For eight years somebody else had decided what came first and what came next, and the moment that disappeared, I discovered I had no idea how to decide it myself. I would sit down to study and, before I knew it, three hours had gone and nothing had happened. What fixed it was embarrassingly small. I gave every task a beginning and an end, so that I always knew which part of the day I was in. As soon as one task finished, I stood up, even for one minute. My mind needed a whistle, the way it always had in the pool. Once I gave it one, the days started to feel like days again.

One of the most useful questions I ask students is not what will you do. It is what will have happened by the time. By the time the exam is over, what will you have done? By the time you start university, what will you have stopped doing? The question works because it makes you plan backwards. Instead of starting from today and hoping the year arranges itself, you start from the end and ask what has to come first. Most students I talk to are surprised by how short the answer is. As long as three or four things happen in the right order, the rest tends to fall into place. The trouble is never the size of the plan. It is the sequence, and almost nobody writes the sequence down.
